unit.title: Materials and Their Structure
unit.blurb: Solids, liquids and gases and the particle model, changes of state, elements and atoms, the Periodic Table, compounds and mixtures.

O1.t: Describe the properties of solids, liquids and gases using the particle model.

O2.t: Describe how the particle model developed and its strengths and limitations.

O5.t: Use the Periodic Table and classify elements as metals and non-metals.

O6.t: Describe compounds, interpret their formulae and apply conservation of mass.

O7.t: Describe mixtures and alloys and compare elements, compounds and mixtures.

captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was created by Atomic Education to help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence. Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 6: Materials and Their Structure.
A glacier is solid ice. Ice melts into liquid water, and water evaporates into invisible water vapour. What is water made of, and why do its forms behave so differently? Let's find out!
All matter exists in different states: solid, liquid and gas. Water can be solid ice, liquid water or water vapour.
A solid has a definite shape and a definite volume. A liquid has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container. A gas has neither.
Solids and liquids cannot be compressed, but gases can. Liquids and gases can flow; solids cannot.
Here's a use: car brakes push liquid along a tube. Because liquids can't be compressed, the push on the pedal reaches the brakes straight away.
Scientists explain these properties with the particle model: all matter is made of tiny particles.
In a solid, particles are packed very closely in a regular pattern, held by very strong forces. They can only vibrate about fixed positions. That's why a solid keeps its shape and can't be squashed.
In a liquid, particles are still close together and touching, but not in a regular pattern. They vibrate and move around each other, so a liquid can flow, but it still can't be compressed.

In a gas, particles are far apart with almost no forces between them. They move very fast in all directions and spread out to fill any space. The space between them is empty, which is why gases can be compressed.
Our ideas about matter have developed over thousands of years, as scientists built on each other's work.
Over 2000 years ago, Democritus suggested that everything is made of tiny atoms, but he had no evidence.
Around 1800, John Dalton said that everything is made of atoms, like tiny building blocks.
Robert Brown saw pollen grains in water jiggling randomly under a microscope. This became known as Brownian motion.
Albert Einstein explained it: invisible particles of water keep hitting the grains. Later, Jean Perrin's experiments matched Einstein's predictions.
Scientists such as Abdus Salam continued to deepen our understanding of particles. Models keep changing as new evidence appears.
The particle model is very useful because it explains what we observe. Ice is hard because its particles vibrate in fixed places, and water is runny because its particles move around each other.
But like every model, it is a simplified picture. It shows all particles as identical balls, yet real particles of different substances have different sizes and shapes.
It also assumes particles don't affect each other, but the attractive forces between them do change how they behave.

q.prompt: The flat part of a heating graph at 0 °C shows…

captions: Matter can change from one state to another. These are called changes of state, like butter melting in a hot pan.
A solid turns into a liquid by melting, like chocolate in your hand. A liquid turns into a solid by freezing, like rain freezing into ice.
A liquid turns into a gas by evaporation or boiling, and a gas turns back into a liquid by condensation, like water droplets on a cold glass.
In a change of state, only the arrangement, closeness and movement of the particles change. The particles themselves stay the same, so no new substance is made.
Let's look closely at melting. In a solid, particles vibrate in fixed places. When the solid is heated, they gain energy and vibrate faster.

Eventually they have enough energy to overcome the forces holding them, and start moving around each other. The solid has melted. The temperature at which this happens is the melting point. Pure aluminium melts at 660 degrees Celsius.
Freezing is the opposite. When a liquid is cooled, its particles lose energy, slow down and move closer together.
They get locked into a regular arrangement and can only vibrate. The liquid has become a solid. A substance's freezing point is the same as its melting point.
When a liquid is heated, its particles move faster and further apart. Some escape from the surface as a gas. This is evaporation, and it can happen at any temperature. That's why puddles dry up.
When a liquid turns into gas all the way through, forming bubbles inside, it is boiling. This happens only at the boiling point. Pure water boils at 100 degrees Celsius.
Condensation is the opposite of boiling. When a gas cools, its particles lose energy, slow down and come together to form a liquid, like the droplets on a cold glass of water.
Let's investigate! Heat crushed ice in a beaker over a Bunsen burner, and measure the temperature every two minutes until the water boils. Remember to wear safety goggles.
Plot the results on a line graph. The temperature rises, then levels off, then rises again, then levels off once more.
While the ice is melting, the temperature stays flat at 0 degrees Celsius. That's the melting point of ice.
While the water is boiling, the temperature stays flat at 100 degrees Celsius, the boiling point of water.

During a change of state, the energy goes into overcoming the forces between particles, so the temperature doesn't rise. With more ice, it would take longer, but the melting and boiling points would stay the same.

q.prompt: How many atoms in an oxygen molecule, O₂?

captions: Here is a model of a water particle: one red oxygen part and two white hydrogen parts.
Using electricity, water can be broken down into oxygen and hydrogen. But oxygen and hydrogen cannot be broken down any further.
A substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical reactions is called an element. Oxygen and hydrogen are elements; water is not.

Everything around us is made of elements. Carbon is found in all living things, copper is used in wires, and neon glows in signs. Hydrogen is the most common element in the universe, and oxygen is the most common in Earth's crust and in our bodies.
Every element has a chemical symbol. Names change between languages, but symbols are the same everywhere. The first letter is always a capital, and a second letter is always lower case.
Many symbols come from the English name: H for hydrogen, He for helium, C for carbon, O for oxygen, Mg for magnesium and Cl for chlorine.
Some come from Latin names: Na for sodium, from natrium; Fe for iron, from ferrum; Cu for copper, from cuprum; and Ag for silver, from argentum.
What is a single piece of an element called? An atom: the smallest part of an element that cannot be broken down chemically. A bar of pure copper contains only copper atoms.
Atoms are incredibly small, much smaller than a virus, a bacterium or a cell.
Trillions of atoms make up one cell. To see an image of atoms we need a special microscope called a scanning tunnelling microscope.
All atoms are tiny, but they are not all the same size. The smallest atom is hydrogen.
Some elements, like argon, helium and neon, exist as single atoms.
But for most elements, atoms join together chemically to form molecules. A molecule made of atoms of only one element is called a molecule of an element.
An oxygen molecule has two oxygen atoms, a phosphorus molecule has four, and a sulfur molecule has eight.
We write molecules using a chemical formula. For nitrogen, N2: the symbol N shows the element, and the small number 2, called a subscript, shows there are two atoms.

captions: Elements with similar properties can be classified into groups. The two main groups are metals and non-metals.

Metals are usually shiny, have high melting and boiling points, and conduct heat and electricity well. They are ductile, so they can be stretched into wires, and malleable, so they can be hammered into shape.
Non-metals are usually dull, have low melting and boiling points, and are insulators. They are not ductile or malleable. Sulfur, carbon and chlorine are non-metals.
The Periodic Table is one of the most important tools in chemistry. It arranges all the known elements in order.
Metals are on the left of the table, and non-metals are on the right.
The rows are called periods and the columns are called groups. The mass of the atoms increases across a period and down a group.
Let's find calcium. It's in the second group and the fourth period, on the left, so calcium is a metal.
Elements in the same group share similar properties. So beryllium, magnesium, strontium, barium and radium behave like calcium. Several are used to give fireworks their bright colours!

The Periodic Table has changed over time. Dmitri Mendeleev is known as the father of the Periodic Table. He was the youngest of fourteen children, and his mother travelled more than 2400 kilometres by horse to find a school for him!
In 1869, he arranged the 63 elements then known by their properties, leaving gaps for elements that hadn't been discovered yet.
About 90 elements occur naturally, and scientists have made more. In 2016, four new elements were added. They had been predicted using the Periodic Table before they were ever made!

q.prompt: 3 g carbon + 8 g oxygen → ? g carbon dioxide

captions: Table salt is made of two elements: sodium, a soft reactive metal, and chlorine, a poisonous green gas.
When they react, they form sodium chloride, a safe white solid that we sprinkle on food! It has completely different properties from the elements it is made of.
Salt is a compound: a substance made of two or more elements chemically combined in a reaction. The elements cannot be separated just by picking them apart.
Water, vinegar, aspirin and baking soda are all compounds too.
We can write compounds with chemical formulae too. In carbon dioxide, CO2, the C with no number means one carbon atom, and O2 means two oxygen atoms. Solid carbon dioxide is called dry ice.
Methane, CH4, has one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. Ammonia, NH3, has one nitrogen atom and three hydrogen atoms.
Hydrogen peroxide, used as a mild antiseptic, has two hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms, so its formula is H2O2.
The atoms in a compound are always in the same fixed proportion. If the proportion changes, it becomes a different substance. With over 100 elements, millions of compounds are possible!

Compounds are formed by chemical reactions, often using heat, light or electricity. We can show a reaction as a word equation: hydrogen plus oxygen gives water. The reactants go on the left and the products on the right.
In a reaction, atoms are rearranged. 3 grams of carbon react with 8 grams of oxygen to make 11 grams of carbon dioxide.
Atoms are never created or destroyed, so the total mass stays the same. The mass of the reactants equals the mass of the products. This is the law of conservation of mass.

captions: When we stir sugar into water, there is no chemical reaction. We can get the sugar back by evaporating the water. Sugar solution is a mixture: two or more substances that are not chemically combined.
Soil is a mixture of sand and clay particles, organic matter, water and air.
Air is a mixture of gases: about 78 percent nitrogen, 21 percent oxygen and 1 percent other gases, plus some water vapour.
Mixtures have no fixed composition. Soil is different in different places. And, unlike pure substances, mixtures have no fixed melting or boiling point.
Steel, brass and bronze are not pure metals. They are alloys: mixtures of a metal with other metals, or with small amounts of non-metals. Alloys are usually stronger and harder than pure metals.
Brass is shiny and is used for trumpets and trophies. Steel is strong and is used for wires, buildings and nails.
Stainless steel is mostly iron, with about 11 percent chromium and 1 percent carbon. It doesn't rust and it's hard, so it's perfect for cutlery.
Let's compare. In models, an element has one type of atom, a compound has atoms of different elements joined in a fixed ratio, and a mixture has different particles that are not joined.
Elements and compounds are pure substances with fixed melting and boiling points. Mixtures are not pure and have no fixed melting or boiling point.
A compound is formed by a chemical reaction and has different properties from its elements. A mixture keeps the properties of its parts and can be separated by physical means.
Some mixtures can become compounds. When a mixture of sodium and chlorine is heated, they react to form sodium chloride, table salt.
Now it is your turn to shine! Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: Which state of matter can be compressed, and why? Pause the video now.
Answer: Gas – its particles have lots of empty space between them.
Question 2: What is the name of the change from gas to liquid? Pause the video now.
Answer: Condensation.
Question 3: How many atoms of each element are in CH₄? Pause the video now.
Answer: 1 carbon atom and 4 hydrogen atoms.
Question 4: Is brass an element, a compound or a mixture? Pause the video now.
Answer: A mixture – it is an alloy.

adv.prompt: * Advanced. Use the particle model to explain why an alloy is harder than the pure metal.
adv.model: In a pure metal the atoms are the same size in neat layers that slide over each other. In an alloy, atoms of different sizes disrupt the layers so they cannot slide easily, making it harder.

kids.d: Solid • liquid • gas – explained by the particle model.
Democritus → Dalton → Brown → Einstein/Perrin. Useful but simplified.
Melting • freezing • evaporation/boiling • condensation. Flat lines on heating graphs.
Cannot be broken down • symbols (Na, Fe, Cu…) • molecules O₂, P₄, S₈.
Metals left, non-metals right • periods (rows), groups (columns) • Mendeleev.
Elements chemically combined, fixed proportion • CO₂, CH₄, NH₃ • mass is conserved.
Not combined, no fixed composition • air, soil • steel, brass, bronze.
